blocks.content: Nearly 59 percent of India's landmass is vulnerable to earthquakes of moderate to high intensity, making systematic seismic zonation vital for structural engineering and disaster mitigation.

items: Zone I does not exist in the current seismic zoning map of India; Zone II is the lowest hazard zone.
Delhi-NCR falls under Seismic Zone IV (High Risk), whereas the North-East region and Rann of Kutch fall under Zone V (Very High Risk).
Questions often test the seismic vulnerability of Peninsular India, highlighting major historic intraplate earthquakes like Latur (1993) and Koyna (1967).

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) classifies India into four seismic hazard zones: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, and Zone V.
Zone I was merged into Zone II in recent revisions, making Zone II the lowest seismic risk region in the country.
Approximately 59 percent of India's landmass is vulnerable to moderate to severe intensity earthquakes.

Zone V represents the highest seismicity zone and encompasses the entire North-Eastern region, parts of Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, the Rann of Kutch, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Major fault lines along the Himalayan convergent plate boundary are responsible for high-magnitude intra-plate and inter-plate seismic activity.
